segments.text: In a neural network, each token starts with a specific row of numbers called an embedding.
As the AI processes a sentence, its layers update those numbers to reflect the surrounding
context.
But this creates an interesting situation.
Those updated numbers rarely perfectly match the starting numbers of any token in the
model's vocabulary.
So if these new coordinates don't perfectly match a known entry in the database, how
can the AI still interpret what the token means?
An exact match isn't actually necessary.
The AI relies on the relationships and the mathematical distances between these numbers.
We can picture these relationships as positions on a map, where nearby locations represent
similar meanings.
Let's look at a standard two-dimensional map.
It uses two numbers, latitude and longitude, to plot a position.
We can add Dallas at 32.78 degrees north, 96.80 degrees west.
Next, Mountain View sits at 37 degrees north, 122 degrees west.
And New York City is at 41 degrees north, 74 degrees west.
Just as latitude and longitude plot physical cities relative to one another in geographic
space, we can use mathematical coordinates to map concepts relative to one another in
a network.
Let's test this map with a new mystery point at 38 degrees north, 120 degrees west.
These numbers don't perfectly match our three established cities.
But by calculating the physical distance on the map, we see that Mountain View is mathematically
the closest location.
We can provide a second test case with another mystery coordinate, 40 degrees north, 76 degrees
west.
Using that exact same logic of proximity, we measure the distance and find that this
second point sits closest to New York City.
Calculating the distance between points gives us a reliable way to identify the closest known
position in a given space, completely removing the need to search for an exact match.
We can apply this same mapping technique to more complex subjects by increasing the
number of coordinates.
Instead of a two-number geographical map, imagine a seven-number taste test.
We can plot items using multiple dimensions, like sweetness, bitterness, and fizz simultaneously.
This diagram groups drinks based on those seven-dimension values.
Coke and Pepsi have highly similar numbers, so they sit near each other in a soft-drinks
neighborhood.
But hot coffee contrasts sharply, high heat and bitterness, zero fizz.
The math plots it far away, in a coffee and tea neighborhood.
Now we introduce mystery drink A. It lands in the soft-drinks neighborhood.
Comparing its values to Coke and Pepsi, most match both, so we check citrus.
Mystery A is 9, Coke is 1, and Pepsi is 10.
With a one-point gap, Pepsi is the closest match.
Next, mystery drink B lands in the coffee neighborhood.
When we measure the gaps, hot coffee is clearly the closest match.
The numerical differences across all seven dimensions are the smallest, linking mystery
drink B directly to hot coffee.
An AI model scales this exact concept exponentially.
Instead of using just seven numbers, its embeddings have thousands of dimensions, with values learned
during training, allowing it to map out incredibly nuanced concepts.
By comparing distances across these thousands of dimensions, the AI doesn't need an updated
token's numbers to perfectly match a database entry.
The token's precise location within a specific conceptual neighborhood tells the model exactly
what it means.
Let's see how this spatial distance logic applies to actual text processing.
Think back to a sentence like,
The tired cat sat on the mat during the May rainstorm.
It soon fell asleep.
On its own, the token IT is ambiguous.
It could refer to the mat, storm, or cat.
But as network layers process the sentence, they update the numbers for IT to reflect its
contextual connection to the token CAT.
This tabletop map shows the update in vector space, featuring distinct neighborhoods for
objects, weather, and animals.
Watch the IT token.
Starting at vector 0.12, negative 0.34, the layers update its numbers.
It moves to coordinates 0.41, 0.06, physically placing it right next to CAT to confirm its
contextual link.
This gives two absolute rules for how models comprehend language.
First, meaning is a position in vector space.
Second, similar meanings usually sit close together.
By dynamically pushing words through this vast, multidimensional map, the AI aligns
their relationships to create deep, contextual understanding.
